To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have demonstrated a method to characterize the degree of spatial X-ray beam coherence with a non-redundent array of slits.
the spatial coherence of a synchrotron beam is a function of the beam parameters, and the spatial coherence can be characterized with a non-redundancy constraint using non-redundantly spaced slits.
the spatial coherence length of the X-ray synchrotron beam can be measured with non-redunderant arrays of apetures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method to characterize the coherence of synchron radiation and to investigate the coherence properties of synchrotrons in a non-invasive way.
the characterization of spatial coherence of a soft X-ray beam.
the development of methods to measure the coherence properties of X-ray beams.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the spatial coherence of XUV synchrotron beam is not fully described by a Gaussian distribution, and that the coherence is better described as a Gaussian distribution with a superimposed Gaussian distribution.
the spatial coherence length of the X-ray source at P04 can be described as a Gaussian function with a FWHM of 2.3 µm, independent of the beam parameters.

the coherence properties of a beam can be characterized by a set of coherence parameters that describe its coherence function, and these parameters can be measured with the help of a non-redundancy array of pinholes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NRAs are a very useful tool to measure spatial coherence and that the method presented in this work is an alternative to the Young's double-pinchole experiment.
we have shown that the coherence properties of the soft X-ray synchrotron beam can be characterized by a simple measurement with the non-redundent arrays.

the spatial coherence of X-rays can be determined with high accuracy using the NRA method and that the NRA method is a powerful tool to characterize the spatial and temporal coherence of X-ray radiation in general.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the degree of coherence is not only dependent on the beam parameters but also on the position of the sample in the X-ray beam.
the coherence properties of the X-ray source can be characterized with a simple experimental setup and a straightforward data evaluation.
the degree of spatial and temporal coherence can be measured with high precision using the presented technique.
